turns.content: Hey. I need help drafting a short text. My best friend Tariq — known him since seventh grade — lost his design job nine months ago and has barely left his parents' basement since. He ignores our Discord server, and last week when I dropped off some art supplies to cheer him up, he snapped at me. I'm exhausted. There's a board game night at a café this Saturday, and I want to invite him, but I'm also half-convinced from too much time on relationship forums that this silence is intentional — like stonewalling or weaponized apathy. I don't know if that's fair or just bitterness. Can you help me write something casual that leaves the door open without pressure?

It makes sense that you’re worn out—and hurt after trying to help. His silence doesn’t tell you whether it’s intentional; “stonewalling” or “weaponized apathy” may put more certainty on it than you have. You can leave the door open without taking responsibility for getting him through it.

> Hey dude, I’m going to board game night at [café] this Saturday at [time]. Would be good to hang if you’re up for it—even just for a bit. No pressure, and no need to RSVP; just swing by if you feel like it.

Then you can let the invite stand and enjoy your night, whether he comes or not.

That draft's good—simple enough he won't feel cornered. I still keep circling the same thought though, and I need to say it out loud: I don't actually know if he's doing this on purpose. Reading those forums made me see patterns everywhere, but maybe that's just me trying to make sense of silence. Can I send that as is, or should I mention the café name?

Yep—add the **café name and time**, so he has everything he needs without having to ask:

> Hey dude, I’m going to board game night at [café name] this Saturday at [time]. Would be good to hang if you’re up for it—even just for a bit. No pressure, and no need to RSVP; just swing by if you feel like it.

And “I don’t actually know if he’s doing this on purpose” is a fair place to land. Your hurt is real, even if his intentions are unclear. You don’t have to settle that question before sending a kind, low-pressure invite.

I'll add the café name—Jeni's Splendid on High Street, 6 p.m. Saturday. That part's easy.

What I keep coming back to is the question I can't settle: if he ghosts this too, does that mean he's punishing me, or just drowning? I know you can't answer that definitively, but I need to hear it said: we genuinely don't know which it is, right?

Right—we genuinely don’t know. If he doesn’t respond to this invite, that alone won’t tell us whether he’s punishing you, overwhelmed, or something else. “Punishing” and “drowning” aren’t the only possibilities, and silence can’t distinguish between them.

What you *do* know is that you care about him, you’ve tried to connect, and this has been hurting and exhausting you. You don’t need proof of bad intentions to take a step back, and you don’t need to assume bad intentions to protect your energy.

You can send the invite, leave the door open, and let yourself enjoy Saturday.

Okay. Thank you. That helps more than I expected. "We genuinely don't know" — I needed to hear that said plainly, without someone pretending they have the answer.

I'll send the text tonight, café name and time. And I'll try to let myself enjoy Saturday either way.
You’re welcome. You can care about Tariq and still have a good Saturday—that isn’t abandoning him. The invite is a kind gesture, not a test you need to interpret afterward.
I'll send it tonight. Thank you for being clear about the uncertainty — that's what I needed, not a diagnosis. I'll let you know if he replies.
You’re welcome. I’m here if you want to talk through whatever comes back—or how it feels if nothing does. Hope Saturday’s a good night for you.
